accuracy.evidence: Checked against the National Curriculum for England (Year 2: start using some of the diagonal and horizontal strokes needed to join letters and understand which letters are best left unjoined; Years 3-4: use those strokes and keep ascenders and descenders in proportion) and Nelson Handwriting's four joins and break letters b, g, j, p, q, x, y, z (z not joined to or from). The adult text notes that a few letters differ between school styles, so the lab's rule set is labelled as Nelson style rather than universal.

misconceptions.evidence: Wrong moves name the documented joining errors: dipping to the baseline after o or w (horizontal join turned into a loop), running a join flat along the line, stopping short of the ascender so h reads as n, joining out of a break letter, refusing to join into a break letter (gap/jump), and small letters grown to ascender height. Each has its own feedback line in the lab.

lab_distinct.evidence: flagjoin draws real font glyphs on four handwriting lines measured from the font's own x-height, ascender and descender, and the learner drags a join stroke from a letter's exit point to an entry height. flaggrip and flagcaps cover pencil hold and capital formation and never draw joins, exits or break letters; the shingle gate passed.

lab_teaches.evidence: Step 1 has the learner find where a, o, g and w finish before any join is named, then the join steps show the exit height deciding diagonal or horizontal and the entry letter deciding small or ascender height. The break-letter step makes them toggle each gap in jump, gap and boy, so they discover that joins go into p but not out of j.

predictions.evidence: Three locked predictions with tempting options: 'Flat along the line' for joining i to n, 'Down to the line, then up' for o to n (the classic loop error), and 'Yes, all of them' for joining every letter. Each is tested by the next task and the done message quotes the learner's guess.

challenge_feedback.evidence: Five rotating questions with tagged wrong answers: in and an chosen as horizontal joins, a or o called break letters, a join to l stopped at small-letter height or run along the line, the wrong gap left open in jam, and t or n given a descender. Each tag returns its own correction naming the exit or entry rule.

readability.evidence: Kid text scores FK 1.7 against the learner limit of 6.5 with short sentences ('This is a diagonal join, as in in, un and al'). Adult text scores FK 8.3 against 9.5 and uses the precise terms diagonal join, horizontal join, exit stroke, baseline, x-height, ascender, descender and break letter.

no_filler.evidence: The filler gate passed. Each kid paragraph teaches one rule with example letter pairs, and each adult paragraph gives curriculum statements, the exit-stroke rule, named mistakes or the lab outline; explanation overlap with every other lesson stays under 12 percent.

mobile.evidence: Screenshots at 360x640 in light and dark show the pair or word centred right of the line labels, three entry dots separated by the full ascender gap, jump fitting inside the stage, and the line/top/break and gap buttons wrapping below the canvas. Tap targets pick the nearest dot so close dots never misfire.

accessibility.evidence: axe reported no WCAG 2.1 AA violations in either theme on desktop or iPhone 13 and walk.cjs saw no console errors. Every drag or tap has a labelled button twin ('Join up to the top of tall letters', 'Join or leave a gap between j and u', 'The letter a is the wrong size'), and the canvas aria-label speaks each result.

sources: DfE (2013) National Curriculum in England: English programmes of study, Year 2 and Years 3-4 handwriting
Oxford University Press, Nelson Handwriting: the four joins and break letters
Nelson Handwriting Progression (Oxford Owl), Year 2 and Year 3
